item.title: VCF 9 で完遂するメインフレーム・モダナイゼーション#2
item.dc:creator: nkondo
item.description:
第二回：メインフレームのアーキテクチャ特性と VCF 9 による実装アプローチ 第一回では、ハードウェアベンダー各社の撤退方針や保守技術者の減少を背景に、メインフレームからの脱却が喫緊の課題であることを整理しました。また、リスクを抑えて移行を進めるためには、パブリッククラウドのマルチテナント環境へ一括移行するのではなく、自社統制を保てる基盤上で段階的なリファクター（自動コード変換と次世代インフラの組み合わせ）を選択することが現実的な解であると述べました。 一方で、業務の中核を担ってきたメインフレームからオープンなインフラへ移行するにあたり、最も懸念されるのは、業務に求められる処理性能や耐障害性を維持できるのかという点です。 連載第二回となる本稿では、メインフレームが長年担保してきた非機能要件の背景を整理したうえで、次世代基盤『VMware Cloud Foundation®（VCF 9 ）』が汎用サーバー上でそれらをいかに実装し、運用性を高めているのかを解説します。   1. メインフレームの堅牢性を支えるアーキテクチャの特性 メインフレームが長年にわたり基幹システムで重用されてきた理由は、ミッションクリティカルな業務を停止させず、大量のトランザクションを確実に処理し続ける高い信頼性にあります。この優れた非機能要件は、単なる計算能力の高さではなく、以下のようなハードウェアレベルのアーキテクチャ特性によって支えられていました。 ハードウェアレベルでのリソース分離 CPU、メモリ、I/O チャネルが厳格に区画化されており、特定業務の負荷スパイクが他の基幹処理に波及しない構造になっています。 低遅延で確定的な I/O 処理 メインプロセッサーとは独立した専用の I/O プロセッサーとチャネル機構により、CPU に負荷をかけずに大量のディスクアクセスを並行処理します。 障害の事前検知と縮退・交代機能 部品レベルのエラーを検知して予備パーツへ自動で切り替えるなど、ハードウェアの冗長構成を前提とした可用性を備えています。 オープン環境への移行プロジェクトにおいて性能や安定性のトラブルが発生する場合、言語変換などのアプリケーション改修や後方互換性の維持に注力するあまり、インフラ層が担っていたこれらのアーキテクチャ特性への配慮が不足しているケースが少なくありません。   2. メインフレーム特性に対する VCF 9 による対応策 メインフレームが持つ堅牢性のうち、インフラ層が担ってきた非機能要件（可用性や負荷分離、I/O 制御など）については、VCF 9のソフトウェア定義（SDDC：Software-Defined Data Center）技術を用いることで論理的に置き換えることが可能です。システム全体の適切なアーキテクチャ設計と組み合わせることで、以下の機能や構成により安定した稼働環境を提供します。   ① 負荷分離：NSX Enhanced Data Path（EDP）による処理効率化とリソース予約 メインフレームのチャネル構造のように、インフラ処理による CPU 圧迫を防ぎ業務処理の性能を確保する手段として、VCF 9 では『Enhanced Data Path（EDP）』を活用します。EDP は、ESX のカーネルレベルでパケット処理を最適化するソフトウェア定義の高速ネットワークデータパス技術です。標準的なパフォーマンス NIC … Continued

item.title: Broadcom Updates VMware Portfolio to Protect and Accelerate Private AI Cloud Deployments
item.dc:creator: prashanth shenoy
item.description:
IT infrastructure and operations leaders are at a tipping point that is driven by AI considerations, such as rising AI infrastructure costs, the new AI-accelerated security landscape, and the rapid advance of agentic AI workloads. This is forcing a fundamental rethink of the infrastructure where AI workloads should run, how to secure all workloads in … Continued

The post Broadcom Updates VMware Portfolio to Protect and Accelerate Private AI Cloud Deployments appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
IT infrastructure and operations leaders are at a tipping point that is driven by AI considerations, such as rising AI infrastructure costs, the new AI-accelerated security landscape, and the rapid advance of agentic AI workloads. This is forcing a fundamental rethink of the infrastructure where AI workloads should run, how to secure all workloads in the new AI-accelerated security landscape, and how to do all of that while meeting increasingly complex compliance and resiliency requirements. The message that appears as a common denominator of these issues is clear: organizations need a cost-effective, secure, and governed path to enterprise AI and better defenses against AI-driven security threats. 

To address these challenges, Broadcom is updating its portfolio of software products to add new or enhance private AI, security, compliance, and data protection capabilities to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), and also to add new solutions to its catalog of Advanced Services for VCF. The new Advanced Services, include the recently announced VMware HyperArmor for a new proactive, real-time defense layer for the ESX component of VCF. Broadcom is also introducing VMware vSphere Express for cost-effective essential virtualization.

Accelerating Private AI Cloud Deployments

With the VCF 9.1.1 release becoming generally available (GA)  on September 3, 2026,  and the next release currently planned for sometime in Q1FY27, the following are examples of new or upcoming features targeted towards accelerating private AI cloud deployments 

  • AI Infrastructure Quickstart   delivers an automated Day 0 deployment experience for customers to smoothly get started with Private AI Cloud, and is planned as part of the next release of VCF, currently estimated to become GA sometime in Q1FY27. It accelerates AI workload readiness by automating foundational infrastructure and software setup through a streamlined vCenter plugin. By handling vCenter cluster deployment, Supervisor configuration, and VKS cluster provisioning, it drastically reduces Day-0 complexity so teams can innovate faster.
  • Multi-tenant Model Sharing is a new feature of VCF, introduced in the VCF 9.1.1 release, that lets customers serve multiple internal units from a single centrally deployed stack with enterprise safeguards such as per-tenant data privacy, security boundaries, and isolated context. Meaning, while the use of this shared model instead of duplicating deployments per tenant inherently cuts infrastructure costs with fewer GPUs and lower TCO, it also  enhances tools and controls for data privacy by design considerations.
  • vSAN Native S3-compatible Object Storage is an upcoming feature of VCF, planned as part of the next release currently estimated to become GA sometime in Q1FY27, that delivers native object storage capabilities to VCF, including for AI projects, cloud-native applications and backup and recovery workloads. It will have self-service provisioning through vSphere Supervisor or VCF Automation.

The above examples highlight Broadcom’s detailed approach to attending to the needs of enterprise customers, from getting AI infrastructure up and running, to optimizing tools to troubleshoot issues, to better sharing AI resources, and optimizing AI performance and token costs

Stronger Defenses for the AI-accelerated Security Landscape

The advancement of Frontier AI models and the broad accessibility of open weight models have changed the three V’s of cybersecurity threats: the volume, velocity, and variety. Stronger security, compliance, and data protection capabilities are now more critical than ever. 

VMware Cloud Foundation is the natural platform for this new landscape, as it already prioritized new feature development that harden security, compliance, and data protection capabilities, – which the latest examples include centralized identity management, data-at-rest and data-in-transit encryption, and VMware vSphere live patching, which applies critical updates to the hypervisor without taking workloads down or placing hosts into full maintenance mode. To further equip customers in this new security landscape, Broadcom is adding the following new capabilities within VCF, as well as adding new solutions to the catalog of Advanced Services available for VCF 

  • VCF infrastructure configuration management and compliance is a new native VCF feature, planned as part of the next release currently estimated to become GA sometime in Q1FY27, that delivers automation and enforcement of VCF infrastructure components as part of VCF Operations. This enables customers to enhance the security posture of their VCF components such as VMware vCenter and VCF Storage, by shifting from reactive to proactive compliance management, as well as configuration drift detection and remediation. Administrators can continuously monitor VCF component settings against key industry benchmarks, including Payment Card Industry (PCI) and the VCF Security Baseline.
  • Confidential computing is a new native VCF capability, made generally available  in the VCF 9.1.1 release, across both AMD and Intel platforms  that, by encrypting data in use at the hardware level, protects sensitive workloads against CPU vulnerability exploitation, VM-cloning data exfiltration, and cross-tenant data leakage. Cryptographic attestation confirms workloads are running in an untampered state, giving customer organizations verifiable security measures where data privacy is critical, including for regulated, sovereign cloud and AI workloads.
  • Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) policy-based connectivity is a new native VCF feature, planned as part of the next release currently estimated to become GA sometime in Q1FY27, that delivers policy-driven connectivity and isolation. Platform engineers can create shared services, define workload isolation and security policies, and apply them consistently across environments, while developers consume network resources through a self-service model without waiting for manual approvals. This accelerates application delivery while maintaining governance and security guardrails.
  • Disaster recovery is a new native feature in VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF) is a new native VCF feature, planned as part of the next release currently estimated to become GA sometime in Q1FY27, that delivers enterprise-scale recovery with orchestration across thousands of workloads, enabling organizations to protect critical workloads and recover quickly from unplanned downtime events, such as from power outages, natural disasters, hardware failures, and human error. 
  • VMware HyperArmor  is a new software offering on the list of available Advanced Services for VCF that was announced at Explore on Tour Frankfurt, that delivers a proactive, real-time defense layer for the ESX component of VCF to protect the hypervisor against AI-accelerated threats. It enables organizations to mitigate vulnerabilities earlier with real-time virtual patching, continuously monitor and protect the hypervisor with positive security guardrails, and neutralize stolen credentials with multi-factor authentication built directly in the SSH login path.
  • VMware Live Recovery  is a new software offering being added today to the list of available Advanced Services for VCF, that delivers disaster and cyber recovery capabilities for VMware workloads, natively integrated with VCF with a secure and performant clean room that is easy to set up and manage, accelerated recovery through rapid iterations and enterprise-scale orchestration, and significant cost savings from streamlined operations, efficient use of infrastructure, and consolidation of multiple tools.
  • VMware Compliance and Configuration Management is a new software offering being added today to the list of available Advanced Services for VCF that  delivers VM and container workload compliance and configuration management capabilities, including continuous compliance enforcement with automated remediation for workloads, helping organizations maintain secure settings at scale against compliance benchmarks such industry benchmarks and standards from Center for Internet Security (CIS), Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), or customer’s own custom standards and benchmarks.

Figure 1: Catalog of Advanced Services for VMware Cloud Foundation

VMware vSphere Express for Essential Virtualization

For customers with smaller environments needing cost-effective essential virtualization, Broadcom is introducing VMware vSphere Express. Built on the reliability, resiliency, and performance of vSphere 9 and available immediately in all regions, vSphere Express delivers core compute virtualization capabilities for customers with 128 cores across all environments with a simplified experience, making it easier for smaller environments on their modernization journey. vSphere Express includes certain essential capabilities, such as:

  • vMotion: Live migration of running virtual machines with improved migration speed and efficiency
  • High Availability (HA): Automated restart of failed virtual machines
  • Distributed Switch: Centralized network management and advanced monitoring
  • vCenter Quick Patch: Low-impact, rapid patch management to maximize uptime
  • Zero-Trust Security: Built-in TPM 2.0 and vTPM 2.0 support

Learn more about vSphere Express on the vSphere web page. 

Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.

What This Means for Your Private AI Cloud

The new updates to VCF features and capabilities, new offerings on the Advanced Services and introduction of vSphere Express show Broadcom’s focused vision of supporting enterprise organizations of all sizes across the globe build their own cost-effective, secure, and governed path to enterprise AI and better defenses against AI-driven security threats. To learn more, talk to your Broadcom account or partner team.

The post Broadcom Updates VMware Portfolio to Protect and Accelerate Private AI Cloud Deployments appeared first on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Blog.

item.title: Demystifying VCF Automation Node Architecture & Load Balancing
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:

The post Demystifying VCF Automation Node Architecture & Load Balancing appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
When deploying VCF Automation, one of the most common points of confusion on the deployment parameter screen revolves around FQDN mappings, Virtual IP (VIP) behavior, and how load balancing operates under the hood. Here is a complete breakdown structure explaining the 3-node High Availability (HA) architecture, the native load balancing layer, and how external GSLB/load balancers fit into the design.

1. The 3-Node Architecture & The 5-IP Requirement

In a standard High Availability (HA) deployment, VCF Installer provisions 3 virtual machine appliances to form a Kubernetes-based container runtime cluster for VCF Automation.

A common question is: If it’s a 3-node deployment, why does the installer require a pool of 5 IP addresses?

  • 3 Active Appliance Node IPs: Assumed in this example as 172.16.50.11, 172.16.50.12, and 172.16.50.13. These are assigned directly to the individual VMs for node-to-node communication and cluster management.
  • 2 Reserved Expansion/Buffer IPs: IPs 172.16.50.14 and 172.16.50.15 stay in reserve within the subnet pool. They are consumed dynamically during non-disruptive rolling upgrades, node redeployments, and day-2 cluster scale-outs.

In addition to the 5 node pool IPs, 2 Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) for VIPs are required outside the IP pool. These two mandatory FQDNs – the VCF Automation FQDN for public user/API traffic and the VCF Automation Services Runtime FQDN for internal management control plane operations – must each map to dedicated static Virtual IP (VIP) addresses provisioned on the same management network.

Per-Node VIPs for External Load Balancing: When integrating an external load balancer (such as AVI) or utilizing round-robin DNS, the external balancer targets individual virtual IP endpoints assigned to each node (Node 1 VIP, Node 2 VIP, and Node 3 VIP). Since VIP 1 already covers Node 1, two additional per-node VIPs are required specifically for Node 2 and Node 3. Keeping all per-node VIPs within the same management subnet simplifies Layer 2/Layer 3 routing, avoids cross-subnet hair-pinning, and ensures seamlessly aligned health probes across the cluster.

2. Decoupling the Two FQDNs

The deployment form requires two distinct FQDN inputs. Both resolve to floating Virtual IP (VIP) addresses on the same management subnet, but they serve completely different purposes:

Do the nodes have 2 NICs? No. Having two FQDNs is a logical ingress design, not a dual-NIC requirement. Both VIPs and all 3 active node VMs operate on a single virtual network interface (NIC 0) connected to the same VCF Management Network Port Group.

3. High Availability (HA) Cluster Architecture

Without External Load Balancer :

Detailed Breakdown of Traffic Paths and Operational Flow:

Direct End-User Ingress (Blue Flow): End users, cloud administrators, and external API callers establish connections directly to the primary VCF Automation FQDN (172.16.50.2) over HTTPS (port 443). This ingress pathway serves the user interface, catalog portal, and public consumption APIs without requiring any intervening third-party load-balancing appliances.

Direct Management Ingress (Green Flow): Management control plane components—specifically SDDC Manager and VCF Operations—route dedicated lifecycle, cluster orchestration, and node maintenance traffic directly to the separate VCF Automation Service Runtime FQDN (172.16.50.3). Isolating this machine-to-machine traffic ensures control plane operations remain uninterrupted by end-user requests.

Embedded Virtual Load Balancer Layer: The native Kube-vip, and Envoy ingress stack automatically hosts both Virtual IPs (VIPs) across the cluster. It monitors node health, handles transparent VIP failover if a node becomes unavailable, and evenly distributes incoming HTTP and API calls across the internal application pods running on Nodes 1, 2, and 3.

With External Load Balancer

Detailed Breakdown of Traffic Paths and Operational Flow:

User Traffic Path (Blue Flow): Inbound external network requests initiated by End Users, Cloud Administrators, or REST API clients are routed to the enterprise-level External Load Balancer / Global Server Load Balancer (GSLB) at IP 10.0.0.100. This GSLB layer acts as the primary global ingress point, performing health checks, DNS routing, and SSL termination or proxying. The external load balancer forwards these incoming user requests to the primary tenant-facing virtual IP address, VIP 1 (172.16.50.50). From VIP 1, traffic enters the native Embedded Virtual Load Balancer Layer, which performs internal Layer 7 ingress routing across the three underlying application node instances.

Control Plane Path (Green Flow): Internal platform orchestration and management components—specifically SDDC Manager and VCF Operations—completely bypass the External Load Balancer and GSLB layer to avoid operational dependencies. They establish direct machine-to-machine management communication via VIP 2 (172.16.50.3). This isolated control plane path handles critical cluster maintenance, lifecycle management (LCM), automated upgrades, and platform telemetry, ensuring management stability regardless of external traffic state.

Cluster Integrity & High Availability: The native Embedded Virtual Load Balancer Layer (utilizing kube-vip, and Envoy proxies) remains active continuously across all 3 nodes. This embedded stack dynamically maintains ownership of VIP 1 and VIP 2, handles local pod-level ingress routing, and ensures automatic floating VIP failover between nodes in the event of an appliance failure.

4. Purpose of Native Load Balancer vs. External Load Balancer

The Native Load Balancer (Internal)

  • What It Is: An embedded load-balancing stack (Kube-vip combined with Envoy proxies) deployed automatically inside the 3 appliance VMs during installation.

Purpose:

  • Binds and hosts the two Virtual IPs (VIP 1 and VIP 2) across the 3 nodes.
  • Handles local failover: if Node 1 goes down, another healthy node automatically claims the floating VIPs within seconds.
  • Distributes incoming HTTP/API calls locally to application container pods running across all 3 VMs.
  • Does It Go Away If You Use GSLB/External LB? No. The native load balancer remains 100% active. Even if external DNS/GSLB directs traffic to the local site, the native load balancer is still required to route requests into the local cluster nodes.

The External Load Balancer / GSLB (Global)

  • What It Is: An external enterprise appliance (e.g., HA Proxy, Avi LB, F5 BIG-IP GTM) that operates at the global DNS layer.

Purpose:

  • Evaluates health probes across multiple geographic data centers.
  • Directs global user traffic to the active local site VIP during cross-site disaster recovery (DR) scenarios.
  • Delegates the user-facing domain (vcfa01.rainpole.io) dynamically without touching site-local management interfaces.

5. When to Use Internal vs. External Load Balancing

6. Upgrade Scenario: Aria Automation 8.18.x to VCF Automation 9.x

When performing an in-place upgrade from Aria Automation 8.18.x to VCF Automation 9.x, the underlying architecture shifts from a legacy deployment model to a Kubernetes-based container runtime cluster integrated with VCF Management Services. Understanding the precise IP address and FQDN requirements is critical for planning subnet allocations and avoiding deployment validation failures.

IP Address Breakdown (Total: 9 IPs Required)

  • 1 x VIP for Automation Runtime Service Platform: Serves as the primary Virtual IP endpoint for management and runtime control plane traffic.
  • 3 x Active Node IPs: Assigned directly to the three appliance virtual machines hosting the Kubernetes container runtime cluster.
  • 2 x Reserved / Buffer IPs: Kept in reserve within the subnet pool to allow non-disruptive rolling updates, node redeployments, and day-2 cluster expansions.
  • 3 x Per-Node VIPs: Individual Virtual IPs allocated per node for local ingress routing, health probing, and external load balancer targeting.

FQDN Requirements (Total: 2 FQDNs)

  • 1 x Runtime Service FQDN: Mapped to the main Automation Runtime Service VIP to handle machine-to-machine control plane calls and lifecycle orchestration.
  • 1 x External Load Balancer / Round-Robin DNS FQDN: Configured on the external load balancer or DNS layer to distribute incoming requests across node VIPs or sites.

item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
What’s Coming Next? The post What’s Coming Next: VMware Cloud on AWS SDDC Upgrade to Version 9.1 appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
What’s Coming Next?

Broadcom is excited to announce that VMware Cloud on AWS cloud offering’s SDDC components will be upgraded to version 9.1, advancing the service to the next generation of the VMware Cloud platform! 

For more than nine years, customers have run their most critical workloads on VMware Cloud on AWS. The upgrade of the SDDC software components of the VMware Cloud on AWS offering to version 9.1 is part of Broadcom’s continued investment in the service, with a focus on the resiliency, security, and long-term supportability of the platform.

Although timelines are still in development, the SDDC upgrade to 9.1 versioned components is planned over the course of three phases: The Early Access phase is intended for customer application-level testing in a non-production organization, and will be considered by nomination only. The General Availability phase, expected some time in calendar year 2027, is when SDDCs with version 9.1 software components will be available as the default build for all newly deployed SDDCs. Soon thereafter, the Fleet Upgrades phase is expected to begin, during which existing customer SDDCs will advance to the latest version. Further details, including feature-level information for the upgrade, will follow in subsequent communications.

Impact

All new and existing SDDCs, including those currently running version 1.26, will upgrade software components to version 9.1 throughout 2027. SDDCs with version 9.1 components are anticipated to be supported on i4i, i3en, and i7i instances, and on future instance types added to the VMware Cloud on AWS service.

The SDDC component upgrade to version 9.1 does not change the current operating model, including Broadcom continuing to maintain patching and lifecycle responsibilities of SDDCs running on VMware Cloud on AWS, 99.9% uptime SLA (99.99% with a stretched cluster), 24/7 global support, SRE coverage, etc.

Patching and upgrades continue as normal in the interim for customers’ existing SDDCs not yet upgraded to the newest SDDC version. The fleet of existing customer SDDCs will proceed through 1.26 versioned releases, with release communications issued as those versions are made available. Customers will receive advance notice before their environments are upgraded to the latest SDDC version.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will my SDDC be upgraded? 

We expect SDDCs with version 9.1 software components to become available as the default build for all new SDDC deployments during calendar 2027. Soon after, the focus will shift to upgrading existing SDDC deployments. Stay tuned for more communication about upgrade timing and scheduling for existing SDDC deployments.

Does this change the VMware Cloud on AWS operating model? 

This is an upgrade of SDDC components of the VMware Cloud on AWS service and has no impact on its operating model. The service continues as Broadcom’s managed SDDC offering for workloads deployed on AWS infrastructure as described in the SaaS Listing.

What happens to SDDCs running version 1.26? 

SDDCs running with version 1.26 will have their software components upgraded to version 9.1 during the Fleet Upgrades phase, currently expected to commence some time in calendar year 2027. 

Will there be an option to remain on version 1.26?

No, the option to remain on older releases is not possible as those SDDCs are delivered as part of a managed cloud offering. Furthermore, upgrades of the SDDCs to version 9.1 are performed by Broadcom as part of the managed service, with advance notice, and require no customer action.

Will the service continue to receive updates before the upgrade? 

Yes. This has no impact on Broadcom’s responsibilities with respect to patching and upgrading SDDCs, regardless of whether they are before or after the SDDC component upgrade to version 9.1.

Which instance types will support the newer SDDC version? 

SDDCs with software components on version 9.1 are anticipated to be supported on i4i, i3en, and i7i instances, in addition to any future instance types that Broadcom may add to the VMware Cloud on AWS service.

What new capabilities will this upgrade bring to VMware Cloud on AWS? 

Upgrading SDDCs to software components on version 9.1 advances the service to the next generation of the Broadcom-managed VMware Cloud platform. Feature-level details are being finalized and will be shared in subsequent communications.

Can I deploy a new cluster with software components on version 9.1 alongside 1.26 clusters in the same SDDC?

No. All clusters within an SDDC need to run the same SDDC version.

Can I deploy a new SDDC with components on version 9.1 alongside existing 1.26 SDDCs? 

Yes. Once the new SDDC version reaches General Availability, and until the Fleet Upgrades Phase is completed for your environments, all new SDDCs will be provisioned with software components on version 9.1 and can run alongside existing SDDCs on version 1.26.

How can my organization be considered for Early Access? 

Contact your account team or the VMware Cloud on AWS product team. Participation for Early Access is at Broadcom’s discretion.

Stay tuned for further updates!

This blog contains forward-looking statements about our product vision. Because software development involves unknowns, including changing market landscape and customer needs, these plans are subject to change without notice. The information in this blog is therefore for informational purposes only, outlines our general product direction, and should not be relied upon in making a purchasing decision. The development, release, and timing of any features or functionality described in this blog remain at Broadcom’s sole discretion.

item.title: When Production AI Hits a Wall, Private Cloud Is the Way Through
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
Enterprises spent the last two years proving that generative AI (GenAI) works in pilots. Moving those same workloads into mission-critical production is where most deployments stall. As organizations scale AI, they quickly discover that “Public clouds charge consumption-based rates for every token generated and every gigabyte transferred, which is ideal for bursty experimentation but expensive … Continued

The post When Production AI Hits a Wall, Private Cloud Is the Way Through appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprises spent the last two years proving that generative AI (GenAI) works in pilots. Moving those same workloads into mission-critical production is where most deployments stall.

As organizations scale AI, they quickly discover that “Public clouds charge consumption-based rates for every token generated and every gigabyte transferred, which is ideal for bursty experimentation but expensive for always-on production services.”1 The operational and financial barriers are real, and they are systemic.

Building on our recent announcements at VMware Explore 2026, where we unveiled the VMware Private AI Cloud built on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), we turn to insights from Jevin Jensen, Research Vice President of Infrastructure and Operations at IDC, to investigate why enterprise AI deployments hit these walls.

The result is an IDC Analyst Connection, sponsored by Broadcom, report titled “Moving Enterprise AI from Pilot to Production on a Private AI Cloud” (Doc #US54945526, November 2026). It maps the systemic barriers IT leaders face and lays out an architectural blueprint for scaling AI securely and cost-effectively.

The Cost Trap in Public Cloud AI

Per-token model execution costs are falling. However, aggregate enterprise AI spend is climbing fast as agentic workflows multiply.

IDC’s August 2026 Intelligent Cloud Survey, cited in the paper, found that “89% of organizations reported unexpected AI-related costs on public cloud or SaaS after go-live.” When workloads shift from occasional testing to round-the-clock inferencing, consumption-based billing, “GPU scarcity” premiums, and data “egress charges” erode projected margins.

The Sovereignty Mandate and Workload Placement

Beyond economics, data sovereignty and privacy compliance have become strategic mandates for IT leaders and boards. Because modern agentic applications and direct tool integrations, such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), grant AI agents deep access to an organization’s most sensitive data, routing this information externally can introduce complex compliance and extraterritorial jurisdiction risks.

However, mitigating these risks does not require abandoning the public cloud. Instead, this IDC Analyst Connection recommends that organizations “Define tiers for data sensitivity (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and map which AI use cases require private infrastructure” and “Prioritize private cloud deployment for workloads that involve personally identifiable information (PII), financial data, or IP-sensitive processes.”1

The Architecture That Works

According to IDC’s August 2026 Intelligent Cloud Survey, “91% of organizations planning to increase private cloud investment in 2027.” Scaling AI on private infrastructure does not require building bare-metal clusters that fragment operations and need hyper-specialized teams.

When data sovereignty or predictable TCO dictates a private AI deployment, “It’s a unified, software-defined platform that supports traditional virtual machines (VMs), containerized applications, and AI workloads under a single operating model.”1

From Variable Costs to Capital Efficiency

We believe the IDC Analyst Connection’s economic analysis indicates that for sustained, predictable enterprise inference, private digital infrastructure provides better cost predictability than consumption-based public cloud models.

Capitalizing and amortizing compute infrastructure removes runaway operational spending. Consolidating AI infrastructure onto VCF also lets enterprises retire fragmented toolsets. Global 2000 companies typically manage four to five separate automation and monitoring tools. Converging onto a standardized VCF platform cuts administrative overhead, speeds up developer velocity, and produces a dependable total cost of ownership (TCO).

Read the IDC Analyst Connection

The Questions and Answers from IDC Jevin Jensen covers the three systemic barriers halting enterprise AI pilots, frameworks for categorizing data tiers to determine private versus public AI deployment, and actionable strategies to implement AI FinOps and curb runaway token consumption.

Download the IDC Analyst Connection Q&A: “Moving Enterprise AI from Pilot to Production on a Private AI Cloud.”

.

1 IDC Analyst Connection, “Moving Enterprise AI from Pilot to Production on a Private AI Cloud,” Doc #US54945526, November 2026.

item.title: From PHP2Shell Alert to Action: Identify and Patch Your Workloads Using VMware Salt
item.dc:creator: rob robertson
item.description:
A vulnerability alert starts the response. Salt helps carry it through discovery, approved repair, and verification—at scale, across your entire fleet. A critical PHP advisory lands. Security wants to know which systems could be affected. Operations need the right packages, the right configuration, and a safe way to replace running workers. Application owners need confidence … Continued

The post From PHP2Shell Alert to Action: Identify and Patch Your Workloads Using VMware Salt appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
A vulnerability alert starts the response. Salt helps carry it through discovery, approved repair, and verification—at scale, across your entire fleet.

A critical PHP advisory lands. Security wants to know which systems could be affected. Operations need the right packages, the right configuration, and a safe way to replace running workers. Application owners need confidence that their services are secure.

Our PHP2Shell use case connects those activities through Salt. The easiest way to understand it is to follow the minion: the Salt agent on a managed server.

The Problem: Patch the system running the affected application

The original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, concern PHP serving web requests. PHP published security releases on October 21. Its October 23 advisory described an additional, configuration-dependent issue, CVE-2026-115560, and recommended disabling session upload progress pending a fix. Our workflow tracks package patching and that mitigation separately. PHP’s advisories explain the affected configurations and response. 

Apache matters when it hosts PHP or passes requests to PHP-FPM. The PHP runtime needs the fix, and affected workers need replacement so that new code and settings take effect. Installing Apache alone does not establish exposure to these PHP vulnerabilities; upgrading Apache alone does not repair PHP.

The goal: Identify the runtime, apply the approved patch, and verify the application before closing the finding.

Follow the Minion: Five steps from identification to remediation

Figure 1 follows one Linux or Windows server. Blue activities are supplied by the Salt states. The other activities show where customer review and validation complete the response.

 Figure 1. One server’s journey through discovery and remediation. 

1. Discover what is installed

The discovery state inventories Linux OS-managed PHP packages. On Windows, it combines package information with checks of configured and common runtime locations, services, and hosting configuration. This helps locate PHP associated with Apache or IIS, including deployments that need explicit ownership mappings.

2. Decide what needs attention

Salt compares the inventory with the selected security baseline and checks the declared upload-progress configuration. The result tells an operator whether the system needs patching, needs mitigation, is mitigated or already patched, or has no PHP detected in the checked scope. Incomplete information produces undetermined and requires review.

Vendor package revisions matter. Ubuntu can deliver a security fix while retaining an older upstream version number. The states account for supported vendor baselines and explicit approved overrides, avoiding unnecessary demands for an upstream version unavailable in the repository. Ubuntu’s PHP security notice lists its corrected packages.

3. Preview and apply the approved patch

The patch state uses configured Linux repositories or approved Windows Winrepo packages and deployment mappings. Operators can preview proposed changes before applying them. Where the additional mitigation is required, Salt disables session.upload_progress.enabled in the declared startup INI files.

On Windows, confirm that exact approved versions are available in Winrepo and that runtime ownership mappings and service names match the existing installation. For deployments already using the supplied fixed-path wrappers, the corrected installer addresses a download failure that could leave Apache and its service missing. It uses .NET downloads with bounded HTTPS redirects while retaining archive checksum and Microsoft signature checks. Other production layouts require their own approved installers; the production setup guide explains both paths.

Configuration coverage must be confirmed by the operator: another startup file, pool, or server setting must not re-enable the feature. A package inventory also cannot prove that a particular application is exploitable.

4. Check configuration and replace workers

Relevant configuration checks gate service actions. Salt coordinates restarts of affected running Apache, PHP-FPM, or configured Windows services and started IIS application pools. Stopped services remain stopped. A configured Windows service must already exist; repair an incomplete installation or correct its mapping before patching. A failed prerequisite blocks dependent work and leaves the failure visible for investigation.

5. Verify the outcome

Run discovery again, confirm active workers, test application health, and validate the finding with the security team’s scanner. A mitigated result means the earlier package fixes are present and the declared workaround is configured; active-worker verification still matters.

A practical demonstration: The Ubuntu lab starts with current repository packages and upload progress enabled, reports needs mitigation, applies the configuration change, and then reports mitigated. The setup and run guide walks through this sequence on a dedicated test minion.

Connect virtual patching with workload remediation

VMware’s Neutralizing PHP2Shell: Stopping Critical PHP RCEs with VMware vDefend and Avi WAF describes network and application protections for the original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Gateway inspection and Avi WAF rules can intercept exploit attempts while teams prepare software updates. 

The Salt use case adds the work inside the managed server, connecting that protection window to a verified repair:

  • Identify the installed runtime. Linux package inventory and Windows package, executable, and hosting checks complement traffic-based visibility. They help operators assess supported managed systems even when PHP version information is absent from HTTP headers. Containers and runtimes outside the discovery scope still require separate coverage.
  • Apply the approved change. Salt updates PHP through the configured repositories or Winrepo mappings, accounts for approved vendor backports, and enforces the upload-progress workaround in the declared INI scope. That configuration step also addresses the separate October 23 advisory; the linked October 21 post discusses the original vulnerabilities.
  • Verify worker replacement and retain evidence. Configuration tests, service actions, and repeatable assessments support the operational handoff. Operators then confirm the effective web runtime, application health, and scanner results before closing the finding.

Teams can use these layers together: apply the relevant vDefend and Avi protections, prioritize affected workloads, run Salt remediation on canaries, and expand after validation. Network controls and Salt jobs require their own configuration; this use case does not deploy WAF rules or correlate security telemetry automatically. The production setup guide covers the workload preparation and verification steps.

From one server to a mature customer response

A mature customer can connect these actions to its security, platform, and change-management processes. Figure 2 shows the proposed operating model around the supplied states.

Figure 2. A proposed customer operating model. Integrations, policy gates, application checks, and recovery procedures require customer configuration.

  1. Scope the finding. Combine advisory or scanner information with Salt assessment results, application ownership, and business criticality.
  2. Prepare and authorize. Review version-controlled states, approve package sources and configuration, and select the maintenance policy.
  3. Start with a canary. Remediate a small representative group; check worker replacement, application health, and scanner results.
  4. Promote in waves. Use configured Salt orchestration to sequence the rollout. Stop promotion when validation fails and follow the approved recovery procedure.
  5. Keep the evidence. Attach assessment results, changes, and validation to the customer’s change or security record, then reassess periodically.

Auto-remediation is possible: these states supply the discovery and repair actions. Customers can configure scheduled assessments or event-triggered workflows to apply approved repairs to eligible systems. Salt’s Reactor responds to events, while Orchestration coordinates actions across systems. Approval routing, ticket updates, load-balancer draining, and rollback procedures must be implemented for the customer’s environment.

The bigger security and compliance opportunity

The same pattern applies beyond PHP. Salt’s configuration management states describe how a system should be configured and apply the changes needed to reach that condition. Teams can use that foundation to:

  • Enforce hardening policies. Manage approved packages, file permissions, accounts, services, and security settings consistently.
  • Detect and correct drift. Schedule comparisons with the approved configuration and remediate deviations according to policy.
  • Coordinate response. Combine targeted execution, configuration changes, and service actions in a reviewed operational workflow.
  • Support compliance evidence. Retain job results and change history, alongside independent validation, to demonstrate how selected controls are maintained.

Customers can choose and implement their own control policies, retention, reporting, and integrations suitable for their organization. Those capabilities support a compliance program through VMware Salt; certification and complete benchmark coverage require their own assessment and remediation.

The files for setup and execution of this use case can be found on github, here.

Scope: This draft describes the supplied PHP2Shell states for the original CVEs and the October 23 upload-progress advisory. Linux source builds, containers, and runtimes outside configured discovery require separate coverage. Later advisories require separate assessment and baseline updates.

item.content:encoded:
In case you haven’t heard, Explore is moving to May 10 – 13 in 2027. Because of this, we are seeking your submissions sooner.

The Call for Proposals for Explore 2027 in Las Vegas Is Officially Open

SUBMIT NOW

We’re going live much earlier in the calendar year than our traditional spring timeframe, so you can claim dibs on your speaking spot before holiday outages, end-of-year change freezes, and fiscal-year deadlines take over your schedule. 

All you need to submit at this time is a title and an abstract.

Presenting at our flagship event in Las Vegas offers an unmatched opportunity to expand your professional profile. You will connect directly with engineers, IT leadership, and industry peers who are actively navigating private cloud operations and modernizing critical infrastructure. 

The Logistics: Mark Your Calendars

  • Submission Window: November 3 – December 11, 2026 (closing at 5:00 PM PST)
  • Event Dates: May 10 – 13, 2027 < DOWNLOAD CALENDAR HOLD
  • Location: Resorts World Las Vegas
  • Who Should Apply?: Broadcom Employees, Customers, Partners, and Community Members of the VMware software ecosystem.

The Content Tracks

Explore delivers focused learning and immediate impact for practitioners managing modern enterprise workloads. We invite system architects, cloud engineers, and technical leads to submit abstracts focused on private cloud, VMware Cloud Foundation, and/or private AI innovations across our four content tracks:

  1. Cloud Infrastructure: Deploy VMs, containers, and AI models on a secure, scalable private cloud.
  2. Modern Apps and Agents: Modernize applications, build, and govern agents to safely deliver software, faster. 
  3. Security: Protect workloads, govern agentic AI, and secure open source software.
  4. Innovation: Harness emerging technologies to unlock the transformative power of innovation

Session presenters receive a complimentary Full Event Pass to attend, providing full access to accelerated certification opportunities, technical sessions, and networking events with peers and VMware software experts.

3 Reasons to Step Up to the Mic

  1. Build Your Personal Brand: Adding “VMware Explore 2027 Speaker” to your resume isn’t just a flex; it’s a career catalyst that builds credibility within the IT ecosystem.
  2. Celebrate Your Successes: in 2026, we saw how VCF 9.1 continues to shape private cloud. Tell us how you actually implement it. Real-world customer journeys are the highest-rated sessions for a reason.
  3. Expand Your Network: Presenting at a flagship event with hundreds of technical sessions means connecting with the best minds in the industry.

Submission Tips for the Win

  • Prioritize Tangible Use Cases: We (and the attendees) love technical deep dives backed by real-world data.
  • Craft a Compelling Title: Think of it as your session’s “elevator pitch.” Make it clear, catchy, and relevant.
  • Address the “So What?”: Explicitly state what value attendees will take back to their desks after the event.

Pro Tip Before Drafting Your Proposal: If you want to review the types of practical, highly-rated content our attendees prioritize, browse the VMware Explore Video Library > Sort by: Most Viewed

  The stage is calling! The #VMwareExplore 2027 Call for Proposals is officially OPEN. Whether you’re a VCF expert or an AI innovator, we want your story in Las Vegas. Apply by December 11!
Share on X

Ready to draft your title and description? 

That’s all you need to submit at this time. The submission window closes December 11 at 5:00 PM PST.

PRESENT AT EXPLORE 2027

 Create a free account and head over to the speaker submission portal today to review proposal details and submission guidelines.

item.content:encoded:
This post walks through Early Join Filtering (EJF) in Tanzu Greenplum 7.9. This extends the “read less, decide early” architecture to hash joins as EJF filters out non-matching rows before payload columns are ever materialized, delivering the query speed of an indexed table without the maintenance overhead.

The post Optimizing Columnar Storage in Tanzu Greenplum, Part 2: Accelerating Hash Joins with Early Join Filtering appeared first on Tanzu.
